newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong needs to boost home supply--analyst.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong needs to boost home supply--analyst.

text.p: Hong Kong's sky-high residential prices could bar some first-time home-buyers from the market if the residential supply is not boosted, a Hong Kong real estate expert warned on Thursday.
"The fundamental problem is still the supply-demand imbalance," David Faulkner, a partner with chartered surveyors and property consultant Brooke Hillier Parker, said at a business luncheon.

Until this was addressed, the market would face continually rising prices, possibly barring some first-time buyers from entering the market, which would ultimately filter through to the whole residential property sector, he said.
Faulkner's remarks came against a backdrop of surging prices in one of the world's most expensive markets.

Last month, a fake bomb was placed outside Hong Kong's legislature to protest rising home prices, a property company paid a record HK$11.82 billion for a major site, and a property agent was knocked unconscious in a scuffle at a flat sale.
Housing is a sensitive issue in densely populated Hong Kong, and the government has promised to work to make housing more affordable and fight speculators.

The incoming Special Administrative Region (SAR) government, which will rule Hong Kong from July 1 when it reverts to Chinese sovereignty, has already set up a task force to study the problems of a runaway residential market.

Last month also saw government measures to boost supply by tinkering with presale regulations. Faulkner said the measures were "fine, but they're trying to treat the symptoms -- not the cause -- of the problem".
In the past two years, the government had released the equivalent of 20,000 new units a year, down from the low 30,000 level in the late 1980s, he said.
"I think probably to redress the balance we ought to be looking at something in excess of 30,000 a year and possibly as high as 35,000," said Faulkner.

Finance secretary Donald Tsang in mid March unveiled plans to increase the supply of new flats in the year to March 31, 1998, to a total of 63,000, but only 21,500 would be produced by the private sector for the open market.
Banks were still keen to lend for residential mortgages, and the supply of units was reduced, Faulkner said.
"It's inevitable that you'll have more money chasing fewer residential units. It doesn't take an economic expert to work out what the impact is going to be on prices," he said.
Young couples often bought a small flat, and upgraded after a couple of years, but if they could not find buyers, they might be forced to stay put.
"I think the concern here really is going to be the ability (of buyers) at the bottom end of the ladder to get on to the ladder," he said.
Faulkner praised the willingness of Hong Kong's incoming rulers to tackle the problem, but warned that it would not happen overnight.
